newsitem.title: KUWAIT: FEATURE-Kuwaiti takes search for POWs on the road.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Kuwaiti takes search for POWs on the road.

text.p: Dream cars cruising the streets of affluent Kuwait do not normally turn heads, but a bright yellow Rolls-Royce daubed with slogans is an eye-catcher.

There's nothing out of the ordinary under the bonnet or behind the tinted glass, but the owner of this limousine hopes slogans painted on the bodywork will grab attention when he drives it through 20 Arab and European states.
Businessman Mohammad Dashti plans the journey in his $180,000 car to drum up support for the 600 Kuwaitis missing since Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of the tiny Gulf Arab oil state.
Accounting for the missing is among demands by the United Nations that must be met before an easing of crippling sanctions imposed on Iraq after its 1990 invasion.
Baghdad says they are "people missing in action". Kuwait calls them "prisoners of war" and insists on their release.
The number of missing seems small but in the context of a population of about 700,000 Kuwaitis they are equivalent to 200,000 Americans or 40,000 Britons.

The emotional issue is part of everyday life in Kuwait where officials begin addresses with passionate calls on God to secure their release and television broadcasts end with "God, we ask You by Your greatest names to free our detainees..."
"I have been detained in Iraq myself and they told me that I would be executed. I know the feeling," said Dashti, who will set off on the road in mid-December.
"DON'T FORGET OUR POWS"

Slogans like "Don't forget our POWs" are painted in bold letters on his Rolls. Similar phrases can be seen all over Kuwait and are also stamped on official documents and aircraft of the national flag carrier Kuwait Airways.
"People tell me 'Why don't you use a camel or a motorcycle instead of a Rolls-Royce, which would make people say Kuwaitis have more money than to know what to do with'?" Dashti said.
"I say, they (foreigners) should say 'Kuwaitis feel nothing is too expensive for such a cause'. I want to attract their attention," he told Reuters.
Iraq, which has long maintained it does not hold Kuwaiti POWs, said in September it would form a committee to investigate the fate of the missing.

"No one can ever imagine the agony of a mother not knowing the fate of her only son for five years," said a Kuwaiti woman. She says her son was snatched by Iraq in the last days of the Iraqi occupation.
"I could have been carrying my grandson by now instead of this," she said, gazing tearfully at a picture of a smiling young figure in a traditional white robe.
"God will make (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein feel this agony at doomsday," she said in a vast hall where pictures of hundreds of the missing are mounted on the walls of a government POW committee.

Diplomats say some of the missing could have been killed during the occupation. But former Kuwaiti captives say they saw some of the missing in Iraqi prisons after the 1991 Gulf War that ejected Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
"This (death) idea crosses my mind every now and again but I tell myself not to believe it," said a 30-year-old Kuwaiti whose cousin is held captive.
THOUSANDS FREED AFTER WAR
One mother said that if her daughter, one of eight missing women, had died "I would have overcome the pain by now".

Iraq released thousands of Kuwaitis after the war but the rest, some diplomats say, were held by Baghdad to secure post-war concessions from Kuwait and its allies -- something that has not happened so far.
Officials from Iraq, Kuwait and its allies meet every month at the border under the auspices of the International Committee of the Red Cross to study files of missing people.
But ordinary citizens say only God can help them.
"I no longer believe governments and organisations can help. Only God can," said a Kuwaiti father on his way to Syria to seek divine help at the Maqam, a Shi'ite Moslem shrine.
